title: The Sultan Who Wrote to Hafez

title_i18n.en: The Sultan Who Wrote to Hafez

subtitle: Poems, Protocols and the Delta’s Reach Across the World
region: Sonargaon, Pandua, Shiraz, Mecca and Medina
moral: Prestige can travel farther by poetry than by cavalry.

sources.citation: Hafez of Shiraz, Diwan, ghazal traditionally linked to Bengal
sources.note: Primary poetic evidence for Bengal's place in the Persian literary imagination.

sources.citation: Yahya ibn Ahmad Sirhindi, Tarikh-i-Mubarak Shahi, c. 1434
sources.note: Nearer narrative source for Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah's reign.

sources.citation: Coins of Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah and Ming Huiyao records of Bengal embassies
sources.note: Material and diplomatic evidence for his sovereignty and foreign contacts.

dialogue.text: In a humid Bengal court of the 1390s, Sultan Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah reached for power not only with armies, but with letters to Hafez of Shiraz and embassies to China.

panels.shot: slow push-in from balcony to distant riverine landscape

dialogue.text: Bengal, c. 1390 CE: a wide green delta, rich with trade, yet far from the famous courts of Delhi, Shiraz and Cairo. Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah asked: how can this edge of the world be seen?

panels.shot: medium interior shot in audience hall

dialogue.text: He inherited a Bengal sultanate balancing many forces: Delhi to the west, the Indian Ocean routes to the east, and a wider Islamic world tied together by merchants, scholars and poets.

panels.shot: close-up on coins spilling onto a table

dialogue.text: On his coins, his name spread with metal: Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah, sovereign of Bengal. But coins speak only where they travel. He wanted the delta named in the language of prestige.

panels.shot: wide shot of courtly literary gathering

dialogue.text: Persian was the tongue of courts. From Anatolia to Hindustan, kings were praised in verse. Ghiyasuddin turned his court toward language and learning, making poets his envoys of reputation.

panels.shot: intimate close-up over shoulder on Azam Shah reading a manuscript

dialogue.text: In those pages he met Hafez of Shiraz, the master of the ghazal. The poet had never seen Bengal, yet his lines coursed through Ghiyasuddin’s court like a deep, shared river of words.

panels.shot: medium shot of writing desk with scrolls and inkpot

dialogue.text: Later tradition tells of a bold act: the Bengal sultan sending verses and a letter to Hafez, seeking the poet’s praise. Whether every detail is exact or not, the link itself is real.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of Azam Shah dictating

dialogue.speaker: ghiyasuddin_azam_shah
dialogue.text: Write that in this distant land of rivers, we too honor the people of verse.

panels.shot: montage-style wide shot transitioning from Bengal to Shiraz skyline

dialogue.text: Hafez did not sail east. But in his Diwan, a ghazal is tied by tradition to a reply sent to Bengal—evidence that the delta had entered the Persian imagination, if only as a distant listener.

panels.shot: wide interior shot of religious scholars and judges

dialogue.text: Another story, told by later chroniclers, praises him for bowing to a qadi’s judgment after a fatal hunting accident. The tale shows how people remembered him: as a ruler mindful of law.

panels.shot: close-up on a judge’s hand over legal text with Azam Shah’s contemplative profile in background

dialogue.text: Historians treat that hunting episode with caution; it cannot be traced as firm institutional reform. Yet it captures the image his age crafted—of a sultan under law, not above it.

panels.shot: dynamic wide shot of port at Sonargaon

dialogue.text: From his ports, boats carried Bengal’s muslin, coins and messages. He looked beyond India: to Mecca and Medina for religious prestige, and to the Ming court in China for diplomatic standing.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye view of embassies departing along river and sea

dialogue.text: Chinese records, the Ming Huiyao, note embassies from Bengal. Earlier scholars called this mere tribute. New readings see something more: an active Bengal diplomacy claiming space in world politics.

panels.shot: evocative mid-shot of pilgrims near desert with imagined Ghiyasuddin overseeing preparations

dialogue.text: Through support for journeys to Mecca and Medina, and through gifts to holy places, he wove Bengal into the spiritual circuits of his time, not only its trade routes.

panels.shot: symbolic wide shot of three scrolls floating over a map from Bengal to China and Persia

dialogue.text: Law, diplomacy, poetry—these became his instruments. Instead of racing to conquer distant lands, he sent coins, letters, students and poems to make Bengal part of the world’s shared stories.

panels.shot: somber interior shot of an empty throne room at dusk

dialogue.text: By around 1411, Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah’s rule ended. Thrones changed hands; cities like Pandua would later decline. But the traces of his choices lingered in coins, chronicles and copied verses.

panels.shot: close-up of a worn Diwan of Hafez with marginal note mentioning Bengal

dialogue.text: To literary scholars, the ghazal linked to Bengal shows how far the sultan reached: his court, once distant from Shiraz, now flickers on the edge of Persian literary memory.

panels.shot: wide shot of modern Bengal landscape dissolving into historical Bengal court

dialogue.text: Coins tarnish and empires fall, but words travel. Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah’s story asks us to see power not only in cavalry and walls, but in law, learning and the courage to let poetry carry a kingdom’s name.
